how: Members call for help drawing the shared mark, adding familiar figures, and placing together at a scheduled time.
A participant judges the rainbow stronger and explicitly connects that imbalance to a proposed move upward.
A direct reply to the drawing call reports partial completion, supporting recruitment followed by reported building without identifying every placer's motive.
The statement that the rainbow has too many people explicitly warrants moving upward, although collective execution remains unverified.
The initial invitation proposes the mark, instantiating the revised starter role independently of whether other people join.
The first recorded proposal already calls for help, so starting and recruitment can be simultaneous rather than separate successive acts.
Members repeatedly propose symbols, lettering and additions rather than settling a single completed design once.
Members report the Nail and Gear present and Brady under construction, supplying descriptions of canvas state rather than placement logs.
A visible-grid request receives a hand-done grid, and coordinates identify where participants should gather.
A requested grid refines an existing template, preserving coordination as an iterative artifact-making practice.
The grid exchange establishes refinement but does not establish that posting a template settled design disagreement.
A member adapts automatic drawing while others object that scripts undermine fun and the event's collaborative spirit.
Automatic placement must accommodate changed plans because a participant attributes vandalism to scripts left running.
A participant reports six hours spent on the logo instead of work, exposing the personal time cost behind collective achievement.
A participant needing rest hands maintenance to others, showing how upkeep is fitted around sleep and fatigue.
A reported glitch appears to allow unlimited blocks, but no coded test establishes that every extra pixel reached the shared canvas.
Explicit design votes put the room within the model's decided-order minority without testing its population frequency or establishing elected leaders.
A brief thank-you answers the report of relaying a proposal and asks for nothing in return.
The bare thank-you answers a relay report rather than a placement call, leaving the proposed call-acceptance preference mechanism untested.
A report of interconnected diplomacy chats does not establish this room's migration into chat or how any unseen chat decided its plans.
Concealment is supported only as unobtrusive placement of a rival flag, with no evidence of coded communications or infiltrating a rival venue.
Members call for defence, request a barrier, repair damage, and hand upkeep to others while resting.
Undoing a centering fix demonstrates interference with planned change, but the coded complaint does not establish keepers' knowledge or whether informing them resolved it.
Automatic vandalism needs distinguishing from uninformed human repair because the concepts identify running scripts without establishing that communication alone would stop them.
One passage explicitly moves from declaring completion to thanking contributors and asking that the work be kept clean.
Maintenance precedes script sharing, but the script announcement does not attribute adoption to attack pressure or insufficient hands.
Participants attribute vandalism to automatic placement and a user acknowledges script responsibility, without proving that every destructive pixel had that source.
A participant proposes moving after the rainbow erases the drawing, linking relocation to a reported loss.
Coordinates locate a proposed gathering point before that particular design has been reported lost.
A member urges claiming space ahead of anticipated takeover, showing preventive siting rather than only relocation after loss.
Members negotiate non-destruction, layout changes, and a trade sacrificing the flag while keeping Grey's face.
Mutual non-destruction and coexistence can be negotiated between factions inside one room rather than only between distinct rooms.
Members change a plan to preserve a neighbour and offer to stop overwriting and help repair another neighbour's image.
An individual's repair offer must remain distinct from collective compliance when the complaint reports repeated overwriting.
Participants request protection, offer restoration, thank a relay, greet a neighbour and report helping another community.
A member reports carrying a proposed border to another room's sticky, while another explicitly describes playing diplomat.
Negotiation also addresses damage from the room's own additions, so neighbours eroding its mark are not the only route to border talk.
Revised plans and attempted repair do not establish a settled border producing sustained restraint across the room.
A proposed trade receives a direct promise to try preserving the face, establishing negotiated help without verifying its execution.
Protection requests and reported help do not establish a complete shortage-driven request followed by delivered outside assistance.
Alliance promotion and reported diplomacy do not establish whether this room joined an operating coalition or shared its decisions.
Calls for protection cannot establish that upkeep pressure produced coalition entry and joint defence.
Reporting a mark in the Grey Blob and playing diplomat does not demonstrate host permission or rules governing a guest work.
Hoping to stop others indicates uncertain coordination but does not explicitly state a mandate limit, deny authority, or request an authorised representative.
No coded disclaimer or refusal establishes either the bounded post-agreement sequence or the contemporaneous authority qualification described in the revised model.
Calling damage a jerk move and condemning destruction supplies moral criticism of covering art without establishing a balanced conquest-versus-preservation debate.
Calling rival-project supporters our traitors and defending them preserves belonging across competing projects without identifying separate named memberships.
Familiar rebel and loyalist identities enter competitive comparisons, calls and admitted interference with the other flag.
Fandom flag lore frames competition and collective belonging, while a call still joins rebels and loyalists in shared lettering.
A participant makes a pop-culture likeness out of damage to Grey's face, without evidence that the joke becomes a shared running gag.
Lore can name a faction within the same room as an attack target while another turn calls for defending that faction.
Members use the canvas to test familiar claims about flag love and challenge that inference through unequal ease of placing flag shapes.
A title labels a swastika a problem, supporting objection to the symbol without establishing its removal or a broader dispute about offensive speech.
A proposal for a dedicated organising subreddit does not establish that a new room formed, acquired followers or developed a shared identity.
Members propose one coordination thread to avoid spam and a dedicated subreddit for serious organising.
The proposed coordination thread explicitly connects containing canvas posts to avoiding spam, without establishing moderator enforcement.
Flag rebellion and familiar jokes do not themselves establish a host takeover or deceptive April Fools framing.
A complaint about canvas spam and an admission of flag vandalism do not link destruction to resentment of the posts.
Members celebrate achievement, claim time spent and remember enjoying collective canvas work.
Participants announce closure, lament an imperfect finish and preserve the corner's appearance in a timelapse.
Members propose episode artwork and advertise successor canvases, without proving that the room collectively adopts either continuation.
Completion and collective thanks appear together in one passage before the handoff to upkeep.
Celebration precedes later recording but no coded statement establishes that celebrating caused the record-making.
Episode-art reuse and replacement-canvas announcements are visible without an explicit link making preservation the cause of continued organisation.
The post-closure cleanup claim supports reported curation, but its destination and any contest between historical versions remain unspecified.
A visitor explicitly says the icon brought them to the room and asks its subject because the sidebar does not explain it.
Imagining a creator's approval supplies audience orientation without establishing contact, solicited notice, press coverage or actual acknowledgment.
The visitor asks what the community is, while the coded concepts do not show questions about canvas rules, controls or picture ownership.
Rest and irritation are visible, but the concepts do not establish quitting under personal strain or repairing an interpersonal quarrel.
A participant admits vandalising the Nail and Gear and another proposes placing Brady over the rebel flag.
Competitive taunts concern internal flag factions, so the contest-in-talk process needs to include rivals within a room.
Recruitment and vandalism are both recorded without evidence that recruitment caused the attack.
The record includes attack, apology and restraint without a coded direct refusal of an attack call establishing the proposed preference mechanism.
Internal truce offers and vandalism admissions do not establish an attack-call-to-truce sequence or its motive.
Rival labels and taunting precede the admission of vandalism, leaving an attack-created named rivalry unestablished.
